questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company redesigns a drug synthesis to use water as a solvent instead of a toxic organic solvent. Which principle of green chemistry does this best demonstrate?

options.text: Using the highest possible temperature
Using safer solvents and reaction conditions to reduce hazards to health and the environment
Maximising the number of reaction steps
Using the cheapest raw materials regardless of toxicity

questions.explanation: One of the key principles of green chemistry is using safer solvents. Traditional organic solvents (like chloroform, benzene, dichloromethane) can be toxic, flammable, and harmful to the environment. Water is non-toxic, non-flammable, readily available, and does not contribute to air pollution. Where possible, replacing hazardous solvents with safer alternatives reduces risk throughout the process.

questions.stem: A reaction produces 150 kg of desired product but also generates 350 kg of by-products that must be disposed of as waste. A green chemistry approach would aim to:

options.text: Find a cheaper way to dispose of the 350 kg of waste
Redesign the reaction to maximise atom economy and reduce the amount of waste by-products
Increase production to make the waste look like a smaller proportion
Ignore the waste since the desired product was made

questions.explanation: Green chemistry aims to maximise atom economy — designing reactions so that as many atoms from the reactants as possible end up in the desired product rather than in waste. High atom economy means less waste, lower disposal costs, and less environmental impact. Addition reactions have 100% atom economy (all atoms incorporated), while many substitution reactions produce wasteful by-products.

questions.stem: A factory uses a catalyst to lower the temperature of an industrial reaction from 500°C to 200°C while producing the same yield. How does this align with green chemistry?

options.text: It does not align with green chemistry because catalysts are chemicals
Lower temperatures mean less energy is needed, reducing fossil fuel use and CO₂ emissions
Catalysts always produce more waste
Lower temperatures always produce less product

questions.explanation: Catalysts are central to green chemistry because they lower activation energy, allowing reactions to proceed at lower temperatures and pressures. This reduces energy consumption, which typically means burning less fossil fuel and producing fewer CO₂ emissions. Additionally, catalysts are not consumed in the reaction and can be reused many times, making them resource-efficient.

questions.stem: Traditional ibuprofen synthesis had 6 steps with an atom economy of about 40%. A green chemistry redesign achieved the same product in 3 steps with an atom economy of about 77%. What practical benefits does this provide?

options.text: The drug works better medically
Fewer steps mean less energy, fewer solvents, and less waste; higher atom economy means more raw material ends up in the product rather than as waste
The only benefit is that it is faster
There are no practical benefits, only theoretical ones

questions.explanation: Fewer synthesis steps mean: less energy for heating/cooling, fewer solvents used and requiring disposal, fewer purification stages, and less equipment needed. Higher atom economy (77% vs 40%) means nearly twice as much of the raw material atoms end up in the desired product rather than as waste. This reduces costs, environmental impact, and the amount of hazardous waste generated.

questions.stem: A green chemistry principle states that it is better to prevent waste than to treat or clean it up after it is created. Which scenario best illustrates this prevention approach?

options.text: Installing expensive water treatment systems at the end of a chemical process
Designing a reaction that uses all its reactant atoms in the product, leaving no waste to treat
Dumping waste in a landfill site
Diluting waste before releasing it into a river

questions.explanation: Prevention is better than cure. Designing reactions with 100% atom economy (like addition reactions) means no waste is generated in the first place. This eliminates the need for costly waste treatment, reduces environmental risk, and is more economically efficient. End-of-pipe treatments (like water treatment or scrubbers) are necessary when waste cannot be prevented, but they are a less ideal solution.
